entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A still-unexplained glowing ball-shaped phenomenon linked to thunderstorms, lasting seconds before vanishing with or without a trace. It is distinct from ordinary branching lightning bolts and has never been reliably captured by instruments, only described by witnesses.
entries.background: The term was coined by the French scientist François Arago in his 1837 work on thunder. It remains a disputed topic in atmospheric physics with thousands of reports but no agreed scientific explanation.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist of the early 19th century who wrote an influential treatise on thunder and lightning in 1837, in which he coined the term for this phenomenon.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: A German senior school official who wrote the only German-language monograph devoted to this phenomenon, published in 1923 and reissued in 2010, drawing on earlier reports such as Arago's.

entries.name: Martin A. Uman
entries.background: A prominent American lightning researcher whose group has used rockets trailing wires to deliberately trigger lightning strikes for controlled study at a Florida test site.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.senseHere: A European research collaboration proposal on lightning physics, bringing together about 30 researchers who agreed that the phenomenon under study genuinely occurs, even without a settled explanation.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: A network of ground sensors across Austria that detects and locates individual lightning strokes, letting researchers match reported sightings to real strikes by time and position.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: A German counterpart to Austria's lightning detection network, used to pinpoint and characterize individual lightning strokes tied to reported sightings.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.senseHere: A lightning discharge that travels between a cloud and the ground, as opposed to one that stays within or between clouds. The article counts how many sightings coincided with this type versus cloud-to-cloud discharges.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: 19th-century geologist and mineralogist who was a member of Vienna's Imperial Academy of Sciences and formally reported his 1868 sighting to that academy.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: An American paleontology professor at Yale and president of the US National Academy of Sciences in the late 19th century, known for pioneering dinosaur fossil research.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German physics professor famous for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrating that particles' magnetic properties come in discrete steps rather than a continuous range.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer who worked at the Jodrell Bank Observatory before becoming a physics professor at the University of Kent.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: A Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who died in 1753 while experimenting on atmospheric electricity, killed by an ungrounded lightning conductor.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or loss of feeling in a limb caused by a lightning or ball lightning encounter, as distinguished from longer-lasting nerve or psychological damage.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician regarded as a founder of modern neurology, a professor in Paris who taught Sigmund Freud and studied patients with nerve disorders following traumatic events.

entries.name: soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: An explanation proposing that when lightning strikes soil, it vaporizes minerals in the ground, creating a floating glowing cloud of burning particles that looks like a ball of fire.
